To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the discrete-time counterpart of the Dai and Singleton (DS) model is a nonlinear DTSM with a closed-form likelihood function, and that habit-based preferences do not match key moments in the conditional distribution of yields.

(1) we develop a rich class of DTSMs, (2) the class of DTSM models nests the exact discrete counterparts of all the affine DTSM models in Duffe and Kan (1998) and Dai and Singelton (2000), (3) the class of models can accommodate nonlinear (non-affine) processes while still leading to closed-form conditional likelihood functions, (4) our approach is general enough to include the equilibrium models with habits, recursive preferences, and

the discrete-time DTSMs with generalized market prices of risk are rich enough to accommodate a large class of continuous-time DTSMs, and that they can accommodate nonlinear dynamics of the state variables under the historical measure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a class of nonlinear discrete-time term structure models (TSMs) that are flexible enough to encompass many of the continuous-time models of the literature.
the estimation of a class of term structure models that are nonlinear in the state vector.
the development of a rich class of nonlinear DTSMs that can be applied to the analysis and estimation of the term structure of interest rates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DTSMs with habit-based preferences are not consistent with the empirical data on bond yields.
the DTSM with a generalized market price of risk is a powerful and flexible framework for modeling the term structure of interest rates.
, while the affine class of models is a very useful tool, it has its limitations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a class of discrete-time nonlinear dynamic term structure model (DTSM).
our model nests a wide range of existing models and can be applied in practice.
we develop a rich class of DTSMs that nests many of the popular models in the continuous-time setting.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when it comes to estimating the conditional distribution of the state variables, it does not matter whether one uses a discrete-time or a continuous-time approach.
the DTSMs we consider can be estimated in a straightforward manner using maximum likelihood techniques.
the DTSM with habit preferences does not match key features in the conditional distribution of zero-coupon bond prices.
